meta.notes: Both Stephen Innes posts are paid-post previews (intro paragraph + 4 takeaway bullets); items extracted from the preview text. Timezone used: UTC+2 as specified.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Goldman's year-end squeeze: liquidation + light positioning + seasonals
items.idea: Goldman's Codacci-Pisanelli and Shah argue the recent liquidation, lighter positioning and supportive seasonal flows could push equities higher into December. Innes' caveat: this is improving market STRUCTURE, not improving fundamentals — and the distinction matters more now than at any point this year.
items.angle: A flow-driven rally after a -6.4% NDX day (Nov 5) is a positioning trade with an expiry date. Size it like one.
items.tweetA: A Santa rally built on 'positioning is light' is a rally with a built-in sell-by date. Once the shorts are covered and the systematic buyers are back, who's the marginal buyer in January? That's the question nobody on the sell side is answering.
items.tweetB: Two weeks ago the Nasdaq had its biggest one-day dollar loss ever. Now Goldman is talking up a December squeeze. Both can be true: flushes create squeezes. Just don't confuse a cleaner order book with a better economy.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Valuation reset + unusually resilient EPS estimates
items.idea: Goldman notes a substantial valuation reset has coincided with unusually resilient earnings expectations. Multiples compressed while forward EPS held — the backdrop is more attractive than headlines (Nvidia CEO exit, blue-wave data center scare) suggest.
items.angle: When P/E falls and E doesn't, the selloff was a discount-rate/sentiment event. Watch whether analysts start cutting 2027 numbers — that's the real tell.
items.tweetA: Prices down, earnings estimates flat. That's not a fundamental selloff, that's a multiple reset. The risk isn't that you bought the dip; it's that the analysts haven't cut yet.
items.tweetB: I've seen 'estimates are resilient' at the start of every earnings downgrade cycle too. The test comes in January guidance season — especially for anyone selling into data center capex in TX, OH and GA.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: The inflation pipeline from 2026's energy shock lands in early 2027
items.idea: Goldman identifies an inflation pipeline from this year's energy shock that could make the opening months of 2027 'considerably less comfortable' — arriving just as investors convince themselves the worst has passed.
items.angle: Pairs directly with HFIR's view that Hormuz flows are falling and the 12m oil spread is +$15. Energy pass-through + backwardation = Q1 CPI risk.
items.tweetA: Energy shocks don't hit CPI when oil spikes. They hit 3-6 months later through freight, utilities and goods prices. The 2026 shock's bill arrives in Q1 2027 — right when the market expects cuts.
items.tweetB: Goldman flags an inflation pipeline into early 2027. Meanwhile the 12-month crude spread is still +$15/bbl. If the oil curve is right and the IEA surplus is wrong, the front end is mispriced.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Goldman's trades beyond equities: front-end inflation and European curves
items.idea: The Goldman roadmap highlights opportunities outside equities — specifically front-end inflation (short-dated breakevens/inflation swaps) and European yield curves — as the way to express the energy-shock pass-through.
items.angle: Front-end breakevens are the cleanest expression of 'inflation pipeline into Q1'. Europe is more energy-import exposed than the US.
items.tweetA: If you believe in a Q1 2027 inflation bump, you don't need to fight equities. Short-dated breakevens are the clean trade. Europe imports its energy — its front end should feel it first.
items.tweetB: Interesting that Goldman's best ideas for a 'Santa rally' note are in rates, not stocks. When the equity strategists hand you a breakeven trade, they're telling you where the conviction actually is.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Innes: buying single-stock selloffs, but wary of leveraged index longs
items.idea: Innes says he's comfortable buying individual names whose earnings prospects are 'considerably healthier than their share prices suggest', but trading indices on high margin into a consensus Santa rally is 'a different animal'. Selection beats beta here.
items.angle: Dispersion regime: stock-pick the damaged quality names, keep index beta light. Long single names / short index is the setup.
items.tweetA: Stock picker's market in one sentence: the individual names are cheap, the index is crowded with seasonality hopes. Long the damage, light on the beta.
items.tweetB: Leverage turns a correct thesis into a margin call. Everyone's 'Santa rally' trade is the same trade. That's precisely why I'd rather own the specific names than lever up the index.

items.title: Hormuz flows and Gulf loadings are falling off a cliff
items.idea: HFIR: escalation in the Oman Lane is producing a structural decrease in oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz, with Gulf loading volumes also dropping sharply — 'tanker attacks = less tankers = less oil'. HFIR is long USO, UCO, BNO.
items.angle: The post-midterm 'peace trade' sold oil; the physical flow data says the opposite. Physical vs narrative divergence is where the trade is.
items.tweetA: Tanker attacks → fewer tankers willing to run the Oman Lane → fewer barrels. No macro model required. The market priced peace after the midterms; the loading data is pricing something else. $USO $BNO
items.tweetB: Every few weeks there's a new Hormuz theory: Iran lost control, cash planes, fake fires. The only theory that matters is shipping insurance. When underwriters stop writing, barrels stop moving.

charts.desc: Hormuz transit flows and Gulf loading volumes, both dropping sharply in recent weeks

items.title: IEA's Q3 'missing barrels': -0.65mb/d stated vs -2.02mb/d observed
items.idea: IEA pegs Q3 2026 balances at a 0.65mb/d deficit, but observable inventory changes were -2.02mb/d — implying 1.38mb/d of 'imaginary surplus' (missing barrels) plugged in to reconcile. HFIR calls the IEA report a set of 'giant rat holes' as the agency declares the market in surplus.
items.angle: Missing barrels in a balance are the classic tell of an agency being wrong on supply. Use the gap as a reason to fade IEA-driven selloffs.
items.tweetA: Do the math: 1.38mb/d of 'missing barrels' x 92 days = ~127M barrels the IEA says exist but nobody can find in a tank. That's not a rounding error, that's a full month of US crude production.
items.tweetB: The IEA says 'surplus'. The inventories say -2.0mb/d. When an agency's balance needs a 1.4mb/d plug to work, I trust the tanks, not the spreadsheet.

charts.desc: IEA oil market balance table showing 2026-27 surplus projections vs Q3 deficit

items.title: 12-month crude timespread +$15/bbl contradicts a ~4mb/d 2027 surplus
items.idea: If the IEA's ~4mb/d 2027 surplus were remotely right, the 12-month timespread would be negative (contango). Instead it's around +$15/bbl backwardation. The curve is openly disbelieving the agency.
items.angle: Curve structure is the market's real-money vote. Steep backwardation + falling flows supports long front-month / roll-yield trades.
items.tweetA: IEA: 4mb/d surplus in 2027. Oil curve: +$15/bbl backwardation. One of them has money on it. Backwardation that steep pays you roll yield to wait for the agency to revise.
items.tweetB: The surplus narrative and a +$15 12-month spread cannot coexist for long. Either the curve collapses into contango, or the IEA quietly revises 2027 in January. I know which one I'd bet on.

items.title: US daily strikes on Iranian surveillance — and CENTCOM has gone silent
items.idea: HFIR says the US has been conducting daily attacks on Iran's surveillance capabilities. Unlike July, when CENTCOM announced every strike, it has announced nothing for weeks. HFIR's read: neither side wants full war, so the result is a grinding, low-intensity conflict that structurally degrades flows.
items.angle: Silence from CENTCOM = deniable escalation. A 'managed' conflict is the worst case for oil bears: no deal, no blowout, just persistently lower flows.
items.tweetA: When CENTCOM announced every strike in July, it was signalling. Weeks of silence while strikes continue is a different message: this is being kept off the front page on purpose. Markets price headlines, not silence.
items.tweetB: 'Neither side wants full war' is usually read as bearish oil. I'd read it the other way: it means the low-grade conflict can last indefinitely, and Hormuz never fully normalizes.

items.title: Post-midterm 'peace trade' sold oil — the market's recurring wrong theory
items.idea: After the Republican midterm 'bloodbath', the narrative became 'peace is coming, Hormuz will be even more open'. HFIR's pattern: oil grinds higher, cliff-dives on a new theory, makes a higher low, then resumes — and admits 'I'm always early'.
items.angle: Higher lows on each narrative flush = trend intact. Use theory-driven dumps as entries.
items.tweetA: The oil tape this year: new theory → cliff dive → higher low → grind up. Repeat. The midterm 'peace trade' is just the latest episode. Chart the lows, ignore the narratives.
items.tweetB: Funny how a domestic US election became an oil supply event. A Democratic House doesn't move a single tanker through the Oman Lane.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Goldman 2027: earnings growth halves, but S&P still to 8,700
items.idea: Goldman's Oppenheimer team expects a dramatic slowdown in earnings growth across major markets in 2027, peak AI capex growth impulse, and an uncomfortable rate environment — yet still forecasts positive returns with the S&P 500 at 8,700.
items.angle: Slowing EPS + positive returns means Goldman is implicitly calling for multiple stability. That only works if yields cooperate — conflicts with the inflation-pipeline note from the same bank.
items.tweetA: Goldman, same week: (1) inflation pipeline makes early 2027 uncomfortable, (2) earnings growth halves, (3) S&P to 8,700. To get all three you need multiples to hold while rates stay sticky. That's the trade I'd question.
items.tweetB: 'The Great Halving' of earnings growth sounds bearish until you remember markets top on peak growth RATE, not peak earnings. If the halving is priced after this correction, 8,700 isn't heroic.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: AI capex at peak growth impulse: hyperscalers vs chip suppliers diverge
items.idea: Goldman argues the AI investment cycle is approaching a transition: the growth impulse of capex peaks, with sharply different implications for those financing the build (hyperscalers) and those supplying the equipment (semis). Value emerges in balance-sheet-strong spenders, while suppliers face second-derivative risk.
items.angle: Peak capex growth = pair trade: long hyperscalers (FCF inflects as capex growth slows) vs suppliers whose revenue tracks capex growth. Watch $NVDA vs $GOOGL/$MSFT.
items.tweetA: When capex growth peaks, the spender's free cash flow inflects up and the supplier's revenue growth inflects down. Same dollars, opposite second derivative. That's the 2027 pair trade.
items.tweetB: Nvidia just lost its CEO, Google shipped four TPU systems in a year, and Goldman says the capex impulse is peaking. If you're long the suppliers, three separate signals are pointing at the same exit.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Growth stocks now cheap vs value and defensives
items.idea: After years of extraordinary premiums, Goldman finds growth stocks beginning to look surprisingly inexpensive relative to traditional value and defensive sectors — 'genuine value in growth' after recent weeks of abandonment.
items.angle: The growth-vs-value relative valuation compression after a selloff is a mean-reversion setup — but it's concentrated in quality balance sheets, not the whole factor.
items.tweetA: 'Value hiding in growth' is the most contrarian sentence a sell-side strategist can write after a -6% Nasdaq day. Which is exactly why it's worth reading twice.
items.tweetB: Growth looking cheap vs defensives isn't a factor call, it's a balance sheet call. Net cash megacaps at a relative discount to utilities that need to fund data center grid buildouts? I'll take that swap.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Goldman favours US and Japan; Asia upside comes with concentration risk
items.idea: Goldman's regional preference for 2027 is the US and Japan, while flagging that opportunities in Asia carry concentration risks investors 'would be unwise to ignore' — i.e. Taiwan/Korea index weights dominated by a handful of AI-supply-chain names.
items.angle: Taiwan and Korea indices are effectively AI-supplier ETFs. If the capex impulse peaks, those are where the second-derivative pain shows up first.
items.tweetA: Buying Korea or Taiwan in 2027 isn't a country bet, it's a 2-3 stock bet on AI capex growth. If you agree the impulse is peaking, the 'cheap Asia' story is a supplier story in disguise.
items.tweetB: US + Japan as the 2027 picks: one has the AI spenders, the other has corporate governance reform and buybacks. Neither depends on capex growth accelerating.

items.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after 33 years; NVDA -14% at open
items.idea: Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two relationships, one with a woman US intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy (WSJ). CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, Harvey Jones becomes the first-ever board chair, and the board has approached Arm's Rene Haas (FT). NVDA fell as much as 14% at the open, below $4T market cap. Parekh calls it the 'Mega-Blip'.
items.angle: Key-person discount on a $4T company with GPUs sold out years ahead: near-term earnings are untouched, the long-term deal machine is not. Watch $ARM if Haas moves.
items.tweetA: GPUs are sold out for years. Nvidia's next 6 quarters of earnings didn't change on Thursday. What changed is who signs the next $100B of deals. The market just priced the key-person discount on a $4T company. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The board approached Rene Haas. Think about that: the CEO of the company Nvidia tried to buy in 2020 might end up running Nvidia. If that happens, $ARM shareholders lose their CEO and the licensing neutrality story gets complicated.

items.title: $140B of Nvidia dealmaking in two months faces a reckoning — the 'Jensen put' pauses
items.idea: About $140B of Nvidia dealmaking — including credit guarantees — in just two months this year now faces a reckoning (The Information). Parekh: the 'Jensen put' that underwrote much of the AI build is on pause; neoclouds, open source and the chip supply chain lose their 'Kingmaker' and 'AI's central bank'.
items.angle: Nvidia credit guarantees backstopped neocloud financing. Without the guarantor's champion, spreads on GPU-backed debt ($CRWV and peers) should widen.
items.tweetA: $140B in two months is ~$2.3B of Nvidia deals per day, some of it credit guarantees. That's not a chip vendor, that's a lender of last resort. The neoclouds just lost their central banker.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching NVDA stock. The hidden signal is in GPU-backed credit. If the guarantor's appetite changes under an interim CEO who was the CFO, refinancing risk moves to the neoclouds.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: 825M shares at $70–78, up to $1.4T valuation, pricing Nov 18
items.idea: Anthropic launched its roadshow: 825M shares at $70–78 on Nasdaq as 'ANT', up to $1.4T valuation, ~$64.4B raised. A larger set of terms was sent to banks Monday and pulled within hours. ~$26B is coming from the AI chip stack, 20% is allocated to retail, the book was reportedly oversubscribed within days. Pricing Wed Nov 18, trading Nov 19; seven co-founders worth ~$18B each.
items.angle: ~40% of the book from chip suppliers is circular financing — they're funding their own customer. Watch IPO day as a sentiment marker for the whole AI complex post-Nvidia shock.
items.tweetA: $26B of a $64B IPO coming from the AI chip stack. Suppliers buying ~40% of their customer's IPO so the customer can buy more of their chips. The circularity isn't hidden anymore, it's in the allocation table.
items.tweetB: The first frontier lab to list prices Nov 18, the same week its prime supplier lost its CEO. If ANT trades well, the AI trade survives the Nvidia shock. If it breaks issue, that's the sentiment top.

items.title: What $1.4T buys: $81B run rate, ~47% q/q growth, ~$900B compute commitments
items.idea: Parekh: the $1.4T valuation buys revenue growing ~47% a quarter, an $81B run rate and nearly $900B in compute commitments. 'Tried and true IPO process with a lot more zeros' — start high, test, find the clearing price.
items.angle: 17x run-rate sales for 4.7x annualized growth is cheap on growth-adjusted terms; the risk is the $900B commitment stack, which is a liability on the other side.
items.tweetA: $1.4T / $81B run rate = ~17x sales. 47% a quarter compounds to ~4.7x a year. If that growth holds even two more quarters, the IPO is priced at single-digit forward sales.
items.tweetB: The number I keep coming back to isn't the $81B run rate. It's the ~$900B in compute commitments: 11 years of current revenue, already promised to suppliers. That's the real balance sheet of the AI boom.

items.title: AI designing AI chips: Anthropic's 15-person chip team, OpenAI's 9-month 'Jalapeño'
items.idea: Anthropic told IPO investors its new 15-person chip design team uses Claude for engineering work, cutting design time vs Nvidia/AMD workflows. Claude Fable 5.1 topped a new ChipAgents/Nvidia chip-design benchmark — at just 16.6%. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 designed three working electronic devices from a one-paragraph prompt. OpenAI designed 'Jalapeño' with Broadcom in nine months.
items.angle: If design cycles compress from 2–3 years to <1, the moat shifts from design teams to fab/packaging capacity. Bullish $TSM/packaging, bearish design-headcount-as-moat. EDA ($SNPS $CDNS) is the swing factor.
items.tweetA: A 15-person team designing custom silicon with AI. Nvidia employs thousands of chip engineers. If design is no longer the bottleneck, the moat moves to TSMC capacity and CoWoS. $TSM $SNPS
items.tweetB: Best model on the chip design benchmark scores 16.6%. That sounds weak until you remember coding benchmarks went from ~15% to ~80% in about two years. Recursive self-improvement just got a silicon lane.

items.title: Google ships four 8th-gen TPU systems in one year; customer list near 100
items.idea: Google launched TPU 8tx (confidential AI, paired with AMD EPYC CPUs) and TPU 8i Max (two 8i chips per package for huge context windows and max compute per rack) — four eighth-gen TPU systems in a year, from a unit that used to ship every two years. Customer list approaching 100. The news landed the day NVDA fell 6.6% and $AVGO and $AMD rose.
items.angle: Specialized TPU family + Broadcom as design partner = $AVGO is the cleaner way to own the Nvidia-alternative trade. AMD gets a CPU win attached.
items.tweetA: Google went from one TPU every two years to four in one year. That's an 8x cadence increase. The chip race isn't Nvidia vs Google, it's annual vs quarterly iteration. $GOOGL $AVGO
items.tweetB: The quiet winner in Google's TPU 8tx: AMD EPYC as the paired CPU for confidential AI. Every non-Nvidia accelerator that ships needs a host CPU. $AMD gets paid on both sides of the 'Nvidia alternative' trade.

items.title: Blue-wave governors in TX, OH, GA ran on pausing data centers — >40% of planned US capacity
items.idea: Democrats won governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia on promises to pause or slow data center construction. Those states hold >40% of planned US data center capacity (Evercore via WSJ), and ~56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote. Parekh: the buildout bends, doesn't break — more costs paid by builders.
items.angle: Data centers became a voting issue. Expect cost-shifting rules (builders pay grid upgrades), favouring on-site generation/behind-the-meter power: $GEV, $BE, fuel cells, SMRs.
items.tweetA: 56% of voters said data centers mattered to their vote. That's a new political constituency: people who hate their power bill. The next phase of AI capex pays for its own grid, which is bullish behind-the-meter power. $GEV $BE
items.tweetB: Texas, Ohio, Georgia: >40% of planned US data center capacity now under governors who campaigned against them. The buildout doesn't stop, it migrates. Watch which states start offering the incentives these three just pulled.

items.title: Nov 5: NDX -6.4%, worst since March 2020; Composite -$2.5T, biggest dollar loss ever
items.idea: The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% on Nov 5 (steepest since March 2020, Axios) and the Composite shed ~$2.5T, its biggest one-day loss ever (WSJ). But hyperscalers fell less, and early signs suggest campaign rhetoric fading once winners take office.
items.angle: Hyperscaler relative strength during a data center policy scare confirms Goldman's spender-vs-supplier split.
items.tweetA: Biggest one-day dollar loss in Nasdaq history, and the hyperscalers — the ones actually building the data centers — fell LESS. The market already told you who it thinks bears the policy risk: the suppliers.
items.tweetB: A -6.4% NDX day on a governor's race result. Not a Fed decision, not earnings, not a war. State-level energy politics is now a top-tier macro variable for US equities.

items.title: United blocks AI agents, following Amazon — the agent access wars begin
items.idea: United Airlines is blocking AI agents from its platform, following Amazon. First reviews of Anthropic's Claude Duet agents are also emerging the same week.
items.angle: If high-value commerce sites wall off agents, agent value shifts to whoever owns direct integrations/APIs. Booking and travel intermediaries face a disintermediation question in reverse.
items.tweetA: Amazon blocked AI agents. Now United. The companies with the most valuable checkout pages are the first to wall them off. Agentic commerce's real bottleneck isn't the model, it's permission.
items.tweetB: Every platform blocking agents is a company betting its margin depends on you seeing the upsell screen. The ones that open APIs to agents first will learn who wins the next distribution war.

items.title: 'Too big to govern': Washington turning, China rushing for chips post-Jensen
items.idea: Parekh's week of ARD episodes flags Nvidia's board, Washington, Beijing and investors all having 'few good options'; Washington turning on Nvidia and China rushing to secure chips amid the spy-probe fallout. Also referenced: OpenAI banking $11B and a revenue jump; an 'AI vs encryption' debate.
items.angle: A China-spy dimension to the CEO exit hands export-control hawks leverage. Expect tighter licensing and Chinese front-running of inventory.
items.tweetA: An Nvidia CEO exit tied to a suspected Chinese intelligence contact is the best gift export-control hawks could receive. China rushing for chips now is rational: the licence window just got shorter.
items.tweetB: Nvidia was 'too big to govern' last week. This week, Washington found the lever. A company that big doesn't get regulated through rules; it gets regulated through its people.
